title: Redis in depth
subtitle: Redis runs your commands one at a time on one thread. Learn what that buys you, what it costs, and what Redis can lose.

c.v: On 20 March 2023, OpenAI took ChatGPT offline. Some users could see titles from another active user's chat history.

Later it found something worse. In the hours before the shutdown, some users could see another active Plus user's name, email address, payment address and the last four digits of their card. OpenAI says this may have affected 1.2% of Plus subscribers active in a nine-hour window.
ChatGPT cached user data in Redis Cluster. Its Python servers used the asyncio version of the redis-py client, with a shared pool of connections.

If a request was cancelled after it was sent, but before its reply was read, the connection kept that reply. The next, unrelated request on the connection read it instead. Usually this caused an error. Sometimes the data looked valid, so one user got another user's cached data.

Since Redis 6.0, I/O threads can read requests, parse them and write replies. The main thread still runs every command. Redis kept this rule on purpose, to avoid races.
They are off by default. The config file suggests them only on machines with 4 or more cores, and only if you have a real performance problem.
I/O threads help with many busy connections. They do nothing for one slow command.

Locks in Redis, and the Redlock debate
The simple lock is one command:
. Release it with a script that deletes the key only if the value is still yours.
On one primary with a replica, a failover can hand the same lock to two clients. The write may not have reached the replica yet.
answers this. A client takes the lock on a majority of, say, 5 independent primaries, within the lock's validity time.
Martin Kleppmann argued that Redlock depends on timing assumptions: bounded network delay,
pauses and clock error. A clock jump can let two clients hold the lock.
His advice: for efficiency, one Redis node is enough. For correctness, use
and a consensus system such as ZooKeeper.
Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez), who wrote Redis, replied. If your storage can check tokens, he says, "you probably don’t need a
at all". A unique random token with check-and-set can work too.

He pointed out that Redlock checks the time again after it gets the majority. He also said pauses after that point hurt "all the distributed locks implementations". On clocks, he replied that Redlock does not need synchronized clocks. Processes only need to count time at about the same speed. He said ops teams can avoid big clock jumps: don't set clocks by hand, and use an ntpd that spreads changes out.
He did agree Redis should move to monotonic time. But he found no other point that broke Redlock's safety, and he rejected the advice to stop using it.

q.v: An engineer runs KEYS user:* on a production Redis with 20 million keys. I/O threads are on. What happens to other clients?

options.v: Nothing. The I/O threads serve them while KEYS runs.
They wait, because one main thread runs every command, and KEYS must finish first.
Redis splits KEYS across all CPU cores, so it ends fast.

why.v: I/O threads only read, parse and write. Commands still run one at a time on the main thread, so a slow one blocks everyone.

q.v: Inside MULTI/EXEC, the second of three commands fails with WRONGTYPE. What happens?

options.v: Redis rolls back the first command.
The first and third commands still run. Redis has no rollback.
EXEC returns null and nothing runs.

why.v: Errors after EXEC are not handled in a special way. The other commands run. A null reply means a WATCHed key changed.

q.v: Redis uses AOF with the default appendfsync everysec. The machine loses power. What can you lose?

options.v: Nothing. Every write is on disk before Redis replies.
About the last second of writes.
Everything since the last daily backup.

why.v: Redis calls fsync about once a second in a background thread, so up to about one second of acknowledged writes can be lost.

q.v: You call SET, then WAIT 1 100, and WAIT returns 1. Is the write now safe from any failover?

options.v: Yes. WAIT makes Redis strongly consistent.
No. It is much less likely to be lost, but a failover can still promote a replica without it.
No. WAIT only checks that the write reached the disk.

why.v: The docs say WAIT does not make Redis strongly consistent. Failover is best effort, so a synchronously replicated write can still be lost.

q.v: Your job holds a Redis lock with a 30 s TTL, then pauses for 40 s in garbage collection. Another worker takes the lock. What protects the data?

options.v: A longer TTL, such as 60 s.
A fencing token, or a version check, that the storage verifies on every write.
Releasing the lock with plain DEL.

why.v: Any lock that expires can be lost during a pause. Only a check at the storage can reject the late write.
